This whole course is called **"AI *for Science*"** — and this is the page where it
all pays off. Back in
[\[2.0\] Language Models](../../02-llms/0-intro-to-llms/index.qmd) we opened with
a claim: the Transformer isn't a *text* architecture, it's a *sequence*
architecture, and much of science is sequences — DNA, RNA, proteins, SMILES
strings. We even name-dropped the example we're about to build up to. Now we cash
that check.

**[GenSLM](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.10.10.511571v2)**
(Genome-Scale Language Models) is an Argonne-led project that trained
GPT-style language models on **genomes** instead of English, and used them to
model how **SARS-CoV-2** evolves — capturing the emergence of variants of concern
*without* wet-lab experiments. It ran across ALCF and NERSC supercomputers and won
the [2022 ACM Gordon Bell Special Prize for HPC-Based COVID-19
Research](https://awards.acm.org/bell). It is the flagship "AI for science on HPC"
result, and by the end of this page you'll have built a (very) small version of it
from scratch.

::: {.callout-tip title="🎯 Learning objectives" collapse="false"}
By the end of this session you will be able to:

1. Explain what a **genome-scale language model** is — the *same* Transformer from
   [\[2.0\]](../../02-llms/0-intro-to-llms/index.qmd), fed nucleotides instead of
   words.
2. Describe **codon tokenization** (3 nucleotides → 1 token) and contrast it with
   **BPE** on text.
3. Build a runnable **codon tokenizer** and a tiny **CodonGPT** that learns
   structure from a synthetic genome — on a CPU, in seconds.
4. Explain **why GenSLM needed a supercomputer**: whole-genome context lengths,
   massive sequence corpora, and billion-parameter models trained across many
   GPUs.
5. Connect that scale story back to the **distributed-training** machinery you
   already learned in [\[1.4\]](../../01-neural-networks/4-distributed-training/index.qmd)
   and [\[2.1\]](../../02-llms/1-parallel-training/index.qmd).
:::

::: {.callout-note title="🧭 Where this fits"}
[\[2.0\]](../../02-llms/0-intro-to-llms/index.qmd) built a mini-LLM from scratch
on tiny-Shakespeare with a character-level tokenizer. **Nothing about that model
was English-specific.** Swap the tokenizer — characters → codons — and point it at
genomes, and the exact same next-token objective becomes a tool for biology. This
page is that swap, taken to its scientific conclusion.
:::

## 🧬 From English to genomes: the same Transformer

A language model learns $P(t_i \mid t_1, \ldots, t_{i-1})$ — the probability of the
next token given everything before it. In [\[2.0\]](../../02-llms/0-intro-to-llms/index.qmd)
the tokens were subwords of English. Here they're pieces of a genome. The
architecture — embeddings, masked self-attention, feed-forward blocks, a softmax
over a vocabulary — **does not change**. Only the alphabet does.

Why is that scientifically useful? A model that predicts the next nucleotide well
has, implicitly, learned the *grammar of the genome*: which substitutions are
plausible, which regions are conserved, how mutations co-occur. That lets you:

- **Generate** synthetic-but-plausible sequences,
- **Embed** a genome into a vector for downstream property prediction, and
- **Score** how "surprising" a real mutation is — the signal GenSLM used to flag
  emerging SARS-CoV-2 variants *before* they were labeled variants of concern.

### Codons: the genome's native tokens

DNA is a string over a 4-letter alphabet — `A`, `C`, `G`, `T`. You *could*
tokenize one nucleotide at a time (a "character-level" model, like tiny-Shakespeare).
But biology already has a natural unit: the **codon**, a group of **3 consecutive
nucleotides** that the ribosome reads to select one amino acid. There are
$4^3 = 64$ possible codons, so a codon vocabulary is tiny and *biologically
meaningful* — each token is a real functional unit, not an artifact of a
compression algorithm.

This is the key contrast with text. GPT-2 uses **Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE)**, which
*learns* a subword vocabulary from data to balance vocabulary size against sequence
length. Codon tokenization needs no learning at all: the genetic code *hands you*
the 64 tokens.

::: {#fig-codon-vs-bpe .column-page}


Two tokenizers, one architecture. BPE *learns* subwords from text; codon
tokenization uses the fixed 64-codon genetic code. Both feed the identical
next-token Transformer.

## ① A codon tokenizer that really runs {#sec-toy}

Everything above is just words until we build it. Following the **toy → real →
scale** rhythm from the rest of this track, let's start with a codon tokenizer
small enough to run on a laptop in a millisecond — pure Python, no downloads.

```{python}
from itertools import product

# The 4 DNA bases. A codon is an ordered triple of bases -> 4^3 = 64 codons.
BASES = "ACGT"
CODONS = ["".join(c) for c in product(BASES, repeat=3)]   # AAA, AAC, ..., TTT
assert len(CODONS) == 64

# Two special tokens: <pad> for batching, <unk> for anything that isn't a clean
# ACGT codon (e.g. an ambiguous base 'N', which real sequencing data is full of).
SPECIAL = ["<pad>", "<unk>"]
vocab = SPECIAL + CODONS
stoi = {tok: i for i, tok in enumerate(vocab)}     # token  -> id
itos = {i: tok for tok, i in stoi.items()}         # id     -> token
vocab_size = len(vocab)


def to_codons(dna: str, frame: int = 0) -> list[str]:
    """Split DNA into non-overlapping codons, starting at reading `frame` (0/1/2)."""
    dna = dna.upper().replace("\n", "").replace(" ", "")
    seq = dna[frame:]
    # drop the trailing 1-2 bases that don't fill a full codon
    end = len(seq) - len(seq) % 3
    return [seq[i : i + 3] for i in range(0, end, 3)]


def encode(dna: str, frame: int = 0) -> list[int]:
    """DNA string -> list of token ids (unknown codons -> <unk>)."""
    return [stoi.get(cod, stoi["<unk>"]) for cod in to_codons(dna, frame)]


def decode(ids: list[int]) -> str:
    """token ids -> space-separated codons (GenSLM prints sequences this way)."""
    return " ".join(itos[i] for i in ids)


# A tiny open reading frame: start codon (ATG) ... stop codon (TGA).
orf = "ATGGCAAAGCTTTGA"
print("vocab size :", vocab_size)
print("codons     :", to_codons(orf))
print("token ids  :", encode(orf))
print("decoded    :", decode(encode(orf)))

# Real genomes contain ambiguous bases; those become <unk> (id 1):
print("with N     :", to_codons("ATGNNNTAA"), "->", encode("ATGNNNTAA"))
```

That's the entire vocabulary of GenSLM's input space in a dozen lines: **66
tokens** (64 codons + `<pad>` + `<unk>`). Compare that to GPT-2's ~50,000 BPE
tokens. A small, fixed vocabulary is one reason genome models can afford very long
context windows — more on that in @sec-scale.

## ② A tiny CodonGPT that learns genome structure {#sec-real}

Now the fun part: feed those tokens to the *same* from-scratch GPT architecture
you built in [\[2.0\]](../../02-llms/0-intro-to-llms/index.qmd) and watch it learn.
We can't train on a real genome here (that's the whole point of the HPC section),
so we use a **synthetic "genome"**: a short, biologically-flavored motif repeated
enough that a tiny model can discover its structure in ~100 iterations on a CPU.

```{python}
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.nn import functional as F

torch.manual_seed(1337)

# A synthetic genome: a repeating motif framed by a start (ATG) and stop (TAG)
# codon. Real DNA isn't this repetitive -- but it lets a *tiny* model learn
# real structure (codon co-occurrence) in seconds instead of GPU-days.
motif = "ATGAAACGCGGGTTTCCCGATTAG"
data = torch.tensor(encode(motif * 200), dtype=torch.long)

# Small enough to train on a CPU in seconds:
block_size = 8     # context window, in *codons*
batch_size = 16
n_embd = 32
n_head = 4
n_layer = 2
max_iters = 100
learning_rate = 3e-3


def get_batch():
    ix = torch.randint(len(data) - block_size - 1, (batch_size,))
    x = torch.stack([data[i : i + block_size] for i in ix])
    y = torch.stack([data[i + 1 : i + block_size + 1] for i in ix])
    return x, y
```

The model is the standard decoder block from [\[2.0\]](../../02-llms/0-intro-to-llms/index.qmd)
— masked self-attention + feed-forward, with residuals and layer-norm — just sized
tiny:

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the from-scratch CodonGPT definition (same as [2.0], sized tiny)"
class Head(nn.Module):
    """One head of masked self-attention."""

    def __init__(self, head_size):
        super().__init__()
        self.key = nn.Linear(n_embd, head_size, bias=False)
        self.query = nn.Linear(n_embd, head_size, bias=False)
        self.value = nn.Linear(n_embd, head_size, bias=False)
        self.register_buffer("tril", torch.tril(torch.ones(block_size, block_size)))

    def forward(self, x):
        B, T, C = x.shape
        k, q, v = self.key(x), self.query(x), self.value(x)
        hs = k.shape[-1]
        wei = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) * hs**-0.5              # (B, T, T)
        wei = wei.masked_fill(self.tril[:T, :T] == 0, float("-inf"))
        wei = F.softmax(wei, dim=-1)
        return wei @ v


class MultiHeadAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_heads, head_size):
        super().__init__()
        self.heads = nn.ModuleList([Head(head_size) for _ in range(num_heads)])
        self.proj = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd)

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.proj(torch.cat([h(x) for h in self.heads], dim=-1))


class Block(nn.Module):
    """Transformer block: communication (attention) then computation (MLP)."""

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        head_size = n_embd // n_head
        self.sa = MultiHeadAttention(n_head, head_size)
        self.ffwd = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(n_embd, 4 * n_embd), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(4 * n_embd, n_embd)
        )
        self.ln1 = nn.LayerNorm(n_embd)
        self.ln2 = nn.LayerNorm(n_embd)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = x + self.sa(self.ln1(x))
        x = x + self.ffwd(self.ln2(x))
        return x


class CodonGPT(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.token_embedding = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, n_embd)
        self.position_embedding = nn.Embedding(block_size, n_embd)
        self.blocks = nn.Sequential(*[Block() for _ in range(n_layer)])
        self.ln_f = nn.LayerNorm(n_embd)
        self.lm_head = nn.Linear(n_embd, vocab_size)

    def forward(self, idx, targets=None):
        B, T = idx.shape
        x = self.token_embedding(idx) + self.position_embedding(torch.arange(T))
        x = self.ln_f(self.blocks(x))
        logits = self.lm_head(x)
        loss = None
        if targets is not None:
            loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.view(B * T, -1), targets.view(B * T))
        return logits, loss

    @torch.no_grad()
    def generate(self, idx, max_new_tokens):
        for _ in range(max_new_tokens):
            logits, _ = self(idx[:, -block_size:])
            probs = F.softmax(logits[:, -1, :], dim=-1)
            idx_next = torch.multinomial(probs, num_samples=1)
            idx = torch.cat([idx, idx_next], dim=1)
        return idx
```

Train it — 100 iterations, a few seconds on a CPU — and track the loss:

```{python}
model = CodonGPT()
optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=learning_rate)

history = []
for it in range(max_iters):
    xb, yb = get_batch()
    _, loss = model(xb, yb)
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
    history.append(loss.item())

n_params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
print(f"CodonGPT parameters : {n_params:,}")
print(f"loss: {history[0]:.3f} (start)  ->  {history[-1]:.3f} (end)")
```

The loss should drop sharply — the model quickly learns the motif's codon
grammar. Now **prompt it with a start codon `ATG`** and let it generate, exactly
as you'd prompt GPT-2 with a few words:

```{python}
prompt = torch.tensor([encode("ATG")], dtype=torch.long)
generated = model.generate(prompt, max_new_tokens=11)[0].tolist()
print("prompt: ATG")
print("generated:", decode(generated))
```

It reproduces the learned motif — the codon-level analogue of GPT-2 continuing a
sentence.

### Scoring how "surprising" a mutation is

This is the payoff hinted at in the intro — the exact signal GenSLM used to flag
emerging variants. A model that has learned the genome's grammar assigns **high
probability** (low *surprise*) to codons that fit, and **low probability** (high
surprise) to ones that don't. We measure surprise as the **negative
log-likelihood** the model assigns to a candidate next codon given the preceding
context — no labels, just the model's own next-token distribution:

```{python}
@torch.no_grad()
def surprise(context_dna: str, next_codon: str) -> float:
    """Negative log-likelihood the model assigns to `next_codon` after `context_dna`.
    High = surprising (the model didn't expect it); low = business as usual."""
    ctx = torch.tensor([encode(context_dna)])       # (1, T)
    logits, _ = model(ctx)                           # (1, T, vocab_size)
    logp = F.log_softmax(logits[0, -1], dim=-1)      # distribution over the next codon
    return -logp[stoi[next_codon]].item()

# In the motif  ATG · AAA · CGC · GGG · ...  the codon after "ATG" is canonically
# "AAA". Compare the model's surprise at the real codon vs. a mutation.
for ctx, canonical, mutant in [("ATG", "AAA", "TTT"),
                               ("ATGAAACGC", "GGG", "CCC")]:
    s_ok = surprise(ctx, canonical)
    s_mut = surprise(ctx, mutant)
    print(f"after {ctx:>10s}:  {canonical} (canonical) surprise={s_ok:5.2f}   "
          f"{mutant} (mutation) surprise={s_mut:5.2f}   ->  {s_mut/max(s_ok,1e-6):,.0f}x more surprising")
```

The canonical codon is almost free (the model expected it); the mutation costs
*many* nats of surprise. Run this across every position of a real genome and the
spikes light up exactly where a sequence departs from what the model learned as
normal — that is variant detection, done with a language model and **zero labeled
data**.

::: {.callout-important title="This is a *toy*, and that's the point"}
Our CodonGPT has ~30k parameters and trained on a repeated 24-nucleotide motif.
The **real** GenSLM foundation models were trained on the **PATRIC** bacterial
gene database and full **SARS-CoV-2 genomes** — millions of real sequences — and
scaled from ~25 million up to **billions** of parameters. Same idea, same
next-token objective, ~six orders of magnitude more everything. Bridging that gap
is exactly what the supercomputer is *for*. That's @sec-scale.
:::

## ③ Why this needed a supercomputer {#sec-scale}

A model this small runs on your laptop. So what makes GenSLM an *HPC* result
worthy of a Gordon Bell prize, and not just "an LLM demo"? Three things, and each
maps onto the distributed-training machinery you already learned.

**1 · Context length over whole genomes.** A single SARS-CoV-2 genome is ~30,000
nucleotides (~10,000 codons); bacterial genomes are far longer. Attention cost
grows **quadratically** with sequence length, so modeling long-range dependencies
across a genome pushes memory and compute far past a single GPU. This is precisely
the pressure that motivates **sequence/context parallelism** from
[\[1.4\]](../../01-neural-networks/4-distributed-training/index.qmd).

**2 · Massive sequence corpora.** Training on the PATRIC gene database plus global
SARS-CoV-2 sequences means streaming enormous datasets through the model — the
data-loading and sharding problem you met in
[\[2.1\] Parallel Training](../../02-llms/1-parallel-training/index.qmd).

**3 · Billion-parameter models.** The largest GenSLM foundation models don't fit
in one GPU's memory. Training them requires sharding parameters, gradients, and
optimizer state across many devices — **ZeRO / FSDP** and **3D parallelism** from
[\[1.4\]](../../01-neural-networks/4-distributed-training/index.qmd), the same
tools the [\[3.1\] Pretraining at Scale](../../03-advanced-llms/1-pretraining-at-scale/index.qmd)
lab drives with `torchtitan`.

| Ingredient | Our toy CodonGPT | Real GenSLM |
|---|---|---|
| Vocabulary | 66 (64 codons + specials) | codon-level, same idea |
| Data | one repeated 24-nt motif | PATRIC genes + SARS-CoV-2 genomes |
| Parameters | ~30k | ~25M up to billions |
| Context | 8 codons | up to whole-genome scale |
| Hardware | 1 CPU, a few seconds | Polaris + Perlmutter, many GPUs |

: From a laptop toy to a Gordon Bell result — same architecture, different scale {.responsive .striped .hover}

::: {.callout-note title="🏆 The real result"}
GenSLM was trained on the ALCF [**Polaris**](https://www.alcf.anl.gov/polaris)
and NERSC **Perlmutter** supercomputers, and the Gordon Bell submission
benchmarked genome-scale training across a range of AI hardware. Beyond raw
scale, the scientific payoff was a **hierarchical** model that combines a
diffusion model for long-range genome context with a Transformer for codon-level
detail, used to *prospectively* model SARS-CoV-2 evolution — identifying variants
of concern from sequence dynamics alone. See
[Zvyagin et al. (2022)](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.10.10.511571v2)
for the specifics (model sizes, throughput, and scaling numbers).
:::

### Loading the *real* pretrained model (run this yourself)

The released 25M-parameter model (`genslm_25M_patric`) is a standard HuggingFace-style
Transformer — the API will feel familiar from [\[2.0\]](../../02-llms/0-intro-to-llms/index.qmd).
It's **not** run at build time here: the weights are a large download (via a Globus
endpoint), so this cell is display-only. On a machine with the weights, it just
works:

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Display-only: requires `pip install git+https://github.com/ramanathanlab/genslm`
# and downloading weights from the project's Globus endpoint (large; not run here).
from genslm import GenSLM

model = GenSLM("genslm_25M_patric", model_cache_dir="./genslm_weights")
model.eval()

# Prompt the language model with a start codon -- exactly like prompting GPT-2,
# but the "words" are codons:
prompt = model.tokenizer.encode("ATG", return_tensors="pt")
tokens = model.model.generate(
    prompt, max_length=10, min_length=10, do_sample=True, top_k=50, top_p=0.95,
    num_return_sequences=2,
    pad_token_id=model.tokenizer.encode("[PAD]")[0],
)
for seq in model.tokenizer.batch_decode(tokens, skip_special_tokens=True):
    print(seq)   # e.g.  ATG GTT ATT TCA TCT GAT TTA CCA ACT
```

Notice the output format: **space-separated codons**, exactly what our tiny
`decode()` produces. The toy and the real thing speak the same language.

::: {.callout-tip title="⚙️ Training it at scale with the tools from this track"}
GenSLM ships its own HPC launcher, but the *pattern* is identical to everything
in [\[3\]](../../03-advanced-llms/index.qmd): build a codon dataset, wrap a
Transformer in FSDP/3D parallelism, and launch across nodes with checkpointing.
Reusing this course's [`ezpz`](https://github.com/saforem2/ezpz) workflow, a
genome pretraining run is the same shape as any other:

```bash
source <(curl -fsSL https://bit.ly/ezpz-utils) && ezpz_setup .venv
uv pip install git+https://github.com/saforem2/ezpz
ezpz launch -n <N> python3 train_codon_gpt.py --data genomes/ --ckpt-interval 500
```

The [\[3.2\] Fault-Tolerant Training](../../03-advanced-llms/2-fault-tolerant-training/index.qmd)
lab explains why that `--ckpt-interval` matters for a multi-day run.
:::

## 🧪 Exercise: robust reading frames

Real sequencing data is messy: it contains ambiguous bases (`N`), and you often
don't know **which of the three reading frames** a fragment starts in. Extend the
tokenizer from @sec-toy to be robust to both.

Write a function `best_frame(dna)` that tries all three reading frames (`0`, `1`,
`2`) and returns the frame whose codon tokenization contains the **fewest `<unk>`
tokens** (ties → smallest frame). Report that frame and its `<unk>` fraction.

::: {.callout-tip title="💡 Show a solution" collapse="true"}
```{python}
def frame_unk_fraction(dna: str, frame: int) -> float:
    ids = encode(dna, frame=frame)
    if not ids:
        return 1.0
    n_unk = sum(1 for i in ids if i == stoi["<unk>"])
    return n_unk / len(ids)


def best_frame(dna: str) -> tuple[int, float]:
    """Return (frame, unk_fraction) for the cleanest of the 3 reading frames."""
    scores = [(f, frame_unk_fraction(dna, f)) for f in (0, 1, 2)]
    return min(scores, key=lambda fs: (fs[1], fs[0]))   # fewest <unk>, then lowest frame


# A messy read: leading junk base + an ambiguous 'N' block.
messy = "GATGNNNAAACGCGGGTTTCCC"
frame, frac = best_frame(messy)
print("per-frame <unk> fraction:",
      {f: round(frame_unk_fraction(messy, f), 3) for f in (0, 1, 2)})
print(f"best frame = {frame}  (<unk> fraction = {frac:.3f})")
print("tokens     :", decode(encode(messy, frame=frame)))
```

The frame that best "phases" onto clean codons has the fewest `<unk>` tokens —
a simple, useful heuristic for aligning noisy reads before feeding them to the
model.
:::

## ✅ Key Takeaways

::: {.callout-tip title="Recap" collapse="false"}
- A **genome-scale language model** is the *same* Transformer as an LLM, trained
  on genomes instead of text. Swap the tokenizer, keep the architecture.
- **Codon tokenization** groups 3 nucleotides into 1 token — a fixed, biologically
  meaningful 64-token vocabulary — versus **BPE's** learned subwords for text.
- A tiny **CodonGPT** learns codon structure from a synthetic genome on a CPU in
  seconds — proving the idea end-to-end.
- **GenSLM** scaled that idea to real genomes and billion-parameter models on
  **Polaris + Perlmutter**, using the *same* distributed-training tools from
  [\[1.4\]](../../01-neural-networks/4-distributed-training/index.qmd) /
  [\[2.1\]](../../02-llms/1-parallel-training/index.qmd), and modeled SARS-CoV-2
  evolution well enough to win a **Gordon Bell Special Prize**.
- This is what "AI for science on HPC" looks like: a general architecture + a
  scientific alphabet + a supercomputer.
:::

## 📚 References & Further Reading

- Zvyagin, Brace, Hippe, Deng, et al., [*GenSLMs: Genome-scale language models
  reveal SARS-CoV-2 evolutionary
  dynamics*](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.10.10.511571v2)
  (bioRxiv, 2022) — the primary paper.
- [`ramanathanlab/genslm`](https://github.com/ramanathanlab/genslm) — the official
  code, pretrained models (`genslm_25M_patric`), and usage examples (MIT license).
- ACM, [Gordon Bell Prize](https://awards.acm.org/bell) — GenSLM won the 2022
  **Special Prize for HPC-Based COVID-19 Research**.
- ALCF, [Polaris](https://www.alcf.anl.gov/polaris) — one of the systems GenSLM
  trained on.
- [\[2.0\] Language Models](../../02-llms/0-intro-to-llms/index.qmd) — the
  from-scratch Transformer this page reuses.
- Vaswani et al., [*Attention Is All You Need*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762)
  (2017) — the architecture underneath it all.

## 🎒 Homework

Turn the toy into something a little more real. Submit **any one** of:

1. **A better toy genome.** Replace the single repeated `motif` with a small
   *mixture* of 3–4 different codon motifs (e.g. concatenate several short
   synthetic "genes"). Retrain CodonGPT and show, from generated samples, that it
   learned more than one motif.

2. **Reading-frame report.** Use your `best_frame()` from the exercise on a batch
   of 5–10 short DNA strings (make some messy with `N`s and leading junk bases).
   Print a small table of `(sequence, best_frame, unk_fraction)`.

3. **Codon vs. character.** Build a *character-level* tokenizer over `ACGT`
   (vocab of ~6) and train the same-sized model on the same synthetic genome.
   Compare final loss and generated samples to the codon model — which learns the
   structure faster, and why might that be?

4. **(Stretch) Run the real model.** On a machine where you can install
   [`genslm`](https://github.com/ramanathanlab/genslm) and fetch the weights, load
   `genslm_25M_patric`, generate a few sequences from an `ATG` prompt, and compare
   its output to your toy's. Submit the sequences.

*Proof* can be terminal output, a saved plot, a notebook, or a short write-up.
The goal: internalize that a genome model is *just a language model with a
different alphabet* — and that scaling it up is exactly the HPC story this whole
course has been building toward.
